summary: The DNS root zone is signed with DNSSEC, so a validating client must be configured with a trust anchor for it. This informational document describes the format and publication mechanisms IANA has used to distribute the root zone trust anchor. It was replaced by RFC 9718.

eli5.summary: To check that a signature is genuine, you need one trusted starting point. This explains how the official root key is published so computers can pick it up and trust it. It has since been replaced by RFC 9718.

questions: where to get the dnssec root key
where to get the dnssec root trust anchor
what is a dnssec trust anchor
what formats does iana publish root anchors in
subtitle: The formats and download locations IANA used to publish the DNSSEC trust anchor for the DNS root zone.

tldr.problem: A DNSSEC validator needs a trusted starting point for the root zone, and the DNSSEC protocol itself does not say how to obtain one.
tldr.mechanism: IANA publishes the root trust anchors as an XML file of key hashes, as X.509 certificates and as certificate signing requests, retrievable over HTTPS or HTTP, with an optional detached CMS signature.
tldr.outcome: Operators can bootstrap root validation from a well-defined source and then use RFC 5011 for updates. This document has been obsoleted by RFC 9718.

today: RFC 7958 is an Informational, Independent Submission document that has been obsoleted by RFC 9718, which is the one to read for current root trust anchor publication.

sections.title: What a Trust Anchor Is and Why It Is Needed
sections.content:
DNSSEC signs DNS data, and a validator checks signatures by following a chain of signatures up to a trust anchor. The reason for trusting a trust anchor lies outside the DNSSEC protocol, but at least one is required for DNSSEC to work.

Publishing the root zone trust anchors is an IANA function performed by ICANN. The document describes the formats and distribution methods used since 2010. Other organizations might publish differently, but most operators and software vendors rely on IANA's anchors.

These formats complement, and do not replace, the automated trust anchor update protocol in RFC 5011. This document describes one way to establish the initial trust anchor that RFC 5011 can then maintain.
sections.eli5: Everything you trust has to start somewhere. The trust anchor is that first thing you simply agree to believe, and everything else is checked against it.

sections.title: The XML Format
sections.content:
The first format is an XML document holding hashes of the root DNSKEY records, consistent with the presentation format of DS records. A TrustAnchor element has an id, a source, a Zone (a single period for the root) and one or more KeyDigest elements.

Each KeyDigest has an id, a validFrom time, an optional validUntil time, and the elements KeyTag, Algorithm, DigestType and Digest. Relying parties SHOULD NOT use a KeyDigest outside its validity range. The KeyDigest id is also used to build the file names of the other formats.

Marshaling the four values gives a DS record. The RFC's example, with key tag 19036, algorithm 8 and digest type 2, becomes a DS record for the root.
sections.eli5: The XML file is a list of fingerprints of the official keys, each with the dates it may be used. You can turn each fingerprint into the standard DNS form with a simple copy-and-paste.

sections.title: Certificates and Signing Requests
sections.content:
The second format is a PKIX certificate for each public key that may be a trust anchor, signed by the ICANN certificate authority. Its public key info holds the Key Signing Key (KSK). The Subject has O set to ICANN, OU set to IANA, a CN of Root Zone KSK followed by the key generation time and date, and a resourceRecord attribute holding the DS record in presentation format.

The third format is a PKCS #10 certificate signing request (CSR) with the same public key info and Subject. The document defines the resourceRecord attribute with an ASN.1 module.
sections.eli5: The same official key is also offered as a digital ID card and as an application form for one. Each says whose key it is and carries the fingerprint inside.

sections.title: Retrieving the Trust Anchors
sections.content:
All files are available over HTTPS and HTTP. The XML set of hashes is at https://data.iana.org/root-anchors/root-anchors.xml. A certificate is at KEYDIGEST-ID.crt and a CSR at KEYDIGEST-ID.csr in the same directory, where the placeholder is the id attribute of the KeyDigest element.

If HTTPS cannot be used, the scheme is replaced with http:.
sections.eli5: There is one web address for the list and a predictable address for each individual key, built from its name.

sections.title: Accepting and Verifying Trust Anchors
sections.content:
Validator operators may accept or reject the anchors under any policy they like. To help them check content and origin, IANA signs the XML file with a detached CMS signature that chains to an ICANN-controlled CA, at root-anchors.p7s. The ICANN CA is not itself a DNSSEC trust anchor, and it cannot verify the origin of the CSR format. A detached OpenPGP signature was provided for the first publication but IANA indicated it would not use it in future.

Retrieval over TLS gives further assurance. If a system trusts the CA used for data.iana.org, HTTPS SHOULD be used instead of HTTP.

Since many DNSSEC clients configure only IANA-issued anchors, reliable publication matters. The only IANA action is a new value, 70, in the SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier registry.
sections.eli5: Because everyone relies on this one list, it comes with a tamper-proof seal and is served over a secure connection so you can tell it is the real thing.

sections.title: Historical Note
sections.content:
The first KSK for the root zone was generated at a key ceremony at an ICANN Key Management Facility in Culpeper, Virginia, USA on 2010-06-16. It entered production at a second ceremony in El Segundo, California, USA on 2010-07-12, and the resulting trust anchor was first published on 2010-07-15.

The RFC also says IANA intended to change the formats and distribution methods in the future and would announce any change on its web site.
sections.eli5: The very first official key was made at a special ceremony in 2010 and shared with the world a few weeks later.

items.desc: PKCS #10 request with the same Subject and public key info.
